advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a lifespan-level regression test that drives lifespan teardown with a worker completing in the same event-loop turn as cancellation, asserting shutdown returns bounded (would fail if lines 68-69 revert to asyncio.wait_for).
evidence: src/rebar/opcert_service/app.py:67-69: 'with contextlib.suppress(asyncio.TimeoutError, TimeoutError): / async with asyncio.timeout(_shutdown_cancel_seconds(app)): / await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)'
Commit message: 'lifespan additionally moves off asyncio.wait_for to asyncio.timeout ... removing the last 86296-susceptible call site.'

The two race tests (test_worker_records_job_timeout, test_worker_cancellation_survives_job_completion_race) call app_module._worker(fake_app) directly (lines 209, 258) and never enter lifespan's teardown, so they exercise _worker, not the changed lifespan gather.

test_shutdown_does_not_wait_for_an_in_flight_job (line 336) asserts only that shutdown does not join the executor thread ('assert not finished.is_set()', line 372); it does not assert lifespan returns bounded when a worker completes in the same turn as cancellation, so it would still pass with the old wait_for at lines 68-69.

Named violating input: a worker task whose _offload coroutine returns a completed record in the same event-loop turn as lifespan's task.cancel() (line 60) — the exact 86296 scenario the added lines guard — is never fed through lifespan by any test.
advisory.finding: The lifespan teardown change (asyncio.wait_for -> asyncio.timeout at app.py:64-69), which the commit states removes 'the last 86296-susceptible call site', has no test exercising it: no test drives lifespan's finally-block gather with a worker task whose _offload body completes in the same event-loop turn that task.cancel() fires. Reverting lines 68-69 to the prior asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.gather(...)) form would fail no test in the suite.
scenarios: A future refactor reintroduces asyncio.wait_for in lifespan teardown; CI stays green while shutdown can strand on py3.11.

dropped.checklist_item: - [ ] Consider having _join_worker retrieve the task's exception (e.g. call worker.exception()/result() when done and it is not CancelledError) so a real worker crash still surfaces instead of being silently dropped.
evidence: Replaced call sites previously read `with contextlib.suppress(asyncio.CancelledError): await worker` (diff hunks at lines ~224 and ~273), which propagated any non-CancelledError worker exception; the new helper does not read `worker.result()`/`worker.exception()`.

ABSENCE: `_worker` re-raises CancelledError but catches all other exceptions internally (src/rebar/opcert_service/app.py:122-143), so in these specific tests the worker exits only via CancelledError and the swallow does not bite today — the concern is the helper's general contract, reused at both real teardown sites.
dropped.finding: The _join_worker teardown helper uses `asyncio.wait({worker}, timeout=bound)`, which never retrieves the awaited task's exception. If a worker task ever terminates by raising a non-CancelledError exception during teardown, that exception is silently discarded (and may only appear as a GC-time 'Task exception was never retrieved' log), whereas the prior `contextlib.suppress(asyncio.CancelledError): await worker` would have re-raised and surfaced it.
scenarios: A future change makes a worker task exit teardown via an unexpected exception; the teardown join swallows it and the test loses the diagnostic that would have named the crash.
